title: Number systems, codes and complements
subtitle: Hardware has two states, so every number, letter and sign is a pattern of 0s and 1s. Learn the patterns, and you can read what a machine is really saying.

sections.title: Why binary
sections.body:
Why do computers use 0s and 1s? Not because engineers like puzzles, but because two states are easy to tell apart. An analog signal varies continuously and picks up noise, like a voice that gets muddier with every phone call. A digital signal is interpreted as only two levels (low = 0, high = 1) with a wide margin between them, so small noise is ignored and copies are exact.

A bit is one binary digit; 8 bits make a byte. And here is the counting rule you will use forever: n bits give 2ⁿ patterns. Each extra bit doubles the number of values, so 10 bits can represent 2¹⁰ = 1024 different values. How many patterns can 6 bits make? Double six times: 64.

worked.why: How many different values can 10 bits represent?

questions.prompt: 6 bits can represent how many distinct patterns?

problems.prompt: What is the minimum number of bits needed to label 100 different items?

keynotes: A digital signal is interpreted as only two levels (low = 0, high = 1) with a wide margin between them, so small noise is ignored and copies are exact.
A bit is one binary digit and 8 bits make a byte.

sections.title: Converting between bases
sections.body:
You write numbers in base 10 without thinking, because you have ten fingers. A computer prefers base 2, and engineers add octal and hex as convenient shorthands. The idea is the same in every base: in base r each place has weight rᵏ. To convert to binary, divide by 2 repeatedly and read remainders upward; from binary, add the weights of the 1s. Octal and hex group bits in 3s and 4s, so conversion is just regrouping.

Convert decimal 25. 25 ÷ 2 = 12 r 1; 12 ÷ 2 = 6 r 0; 6 ÷ 2 = 3 r 0; 3 ÷ 2 = 1 r 1; 1 ÷ 2 = 0 r 1. Read the remainders upward: 25₁₀ = 11001₂. Group the bits and you get octal 31 and hex 19. The same number appears in every code in the figure. Try binary 1011 0110 in hex yourself: the nibbles 1011 and 0110 are B and 6.

sections.title: BCD, excess-3 and Gray
sections.body:
Sometimes you want to keep decimal digits intact inside a machine, for a calculator display or a clock. Three codes help. BCD writes each decimal digit in 4 bits: 25 → 0010 0101. Excess-3 adds 3 to each digit (0101 1000), which is self-complementing. Gray code changes only one bit between neighbouring values (10101 for 25).

Why would anyone want Gray code? Think of a shaft encoder reading a rotating wheel: if two bits had to flip at once, a sensor might catch the wheel half-way and report a wildly wrong value. With Gray code only one bit changes per step, so no glitch between steps can show a wrong value.

questions.prompt: Gray code is useful for shaft encoders because…

choices.text: Only one bit changes per step.

keynotes: BCD writes each decimal digit in 4 bits: 25 is 0010 0101.
Excess-3 adds 3 to each digit (0101 1000 for 25) and is self-complementing.
Gray code changes only one bit between neighbouring values (10101 for 25), ideal for position encoders because no glitch between steps can show a wrong value.

sections.title: Signed numbers
sections.body:
How do you write −25 when you only have 0s and 1s? There are three schemes, and you should know why the third one won. Sign–magnitude: the top bit is the sign. 1's complement: invert all bits. 2's complement: invert, then add 1.

2's complement wins because there is one zero, and addition just works. For −25 in 8 bits: sign–magnitude 10011001, 1's 11100110, 2's 11100111. Build it: +25 = 00011001, invert every bit to get 11100110, then add 1 for 11100111 = −25. A 4-bit word covers −8 … +7. And what is the 4-bit 2's complement of +6? 0110 inverted is 1001, plus 1 is 1010.
keynotes: Sign–magnitude uses the top bit as the sign, 1's complement inverts all bits and 2's complement inverts then adds 1.
2's complement wins: it has one zero and addition just works.
−25 in 8 bits is sign–magnitude 10011001, 1's 11100110 and 2's 11100111; a 4-bit word covers −8 … +7.

sections.title: Adding and overflow
sections.body:
What happens when a result is too big to fit? In 2's complement, add as usual and discard the carry out. Overflow occurs when two numbers of the same sign give a result of the opposite sign (equivalently the carry into and out of the sign bit differ).

See it fail in 4 bits, where the range is −8…+7. 5 + 4 = 9 does not fit: 0101 (+5) + 0100 (+4) = 1001, which reads as −7. The result is negative although both inputs were positive, and that is overflow. So if you add two positive 2's complement numbers and get a negative result, the answer is wrong because of overflow.

worked.why: Result 1001 is negative although both inputs were positive: overflow.

questions.prompt: Adding two positive 2’s complement numbers gives a negative result. That means…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The true sum did not fit.

keynotes: In 2's complement, add as usual and discard the carry out.
Overflow occurs when two numbers of the same sign give a result of the opposite sign (the carry into and out of the sign bit differ).
In 4 bits, 0101 + 0100 = 1001, which reads as −7 instead of +9.

sections.title: Characters and parity
sections.body:
Letters are numbers too. ASCII assigns 7-bit codes to characters: ‘A’ = 65 = 1000001₂, ‘a’ = 97. Unicode extends this to all scripts (UTF-8). And since a flipped bit can turn one letter into another, we add a check: a parity bit makes the count of 1s even (or odd) so a single flipped bit is detected, though not corrected.

Try even parity for ‘A’ = 1000001. It has two 1s, which is already even, so the parity bit is 0 and the byte is 01000001. A single parity bit can detect one flipped bit, but it cannot say which bit it was.

worked.why: Already even, so the parity bit is 0.
